title: SAVA Health App
subtitle: One CGM platform for two opposing users

slides.title: SAVA Health App
slides.standfirst: Reimagining continuous glucose monitoring for two audiences whose needs invert each other: Type 1 diabetes patients who need critical real-time data under stress, and wellness consumers who need motivation and interpretation.

bullets.text: Lead UX Designer, conceptual case study
Two personas, two journeys, two interfaces, one data foundation
Conceptual prototypes, not validated designs

slides.notes: Put the caveat on the cover. It costs nothing and it buys credibility for everything that follows.

slides.title: One platform, two audiences
slides.notes: Establishing shot. Ten seconds, then move to the data stream.

slides.title: One data stream, arriving every few minutes, all day
slides.standfirst: Continuous glucose monitoring produces a live trace. Both audiences receive exactly the same numbers — and need almost opposite things done to them.

figure.caption: Live trace with target band and forward prediction

slides.notes: Let this run. The dashed forward segment is the prediction — point at it, because it becomes the T1D design decision later.

slides.title: Medical accuracy, at the cost of clarity
slides.standfirst: Applications such as Dexcom G6 optimise for correctness and fall short on visual clarity and intuitive insight. The critique identified four specific failures.

bullets.text: Competing information on the home screen.
The most critical element — the trend graph — was small and hard to read.
Raw data presented without actionable guidance.
The history screen was a flat list, making pattern-finding difficult.

items.alt: The incumbent CGM application home screen
items.label: Home

items.alt: The incumbent CGM application history screen
items.label: History

slides.notes: Be fair to the incumbent. It is medically excellent; the critique is about hierarchy and interpretation, not accuracy.

slides.title: Journey mapping showed the two audiences failing differently

bullets.text: Anxiety over a single number. Uncertainty about what a trend means. Forgotten logging events. Data scattered across screens.
No single motivating metric. Disconnected data points. No real-time feedback on actions. No clear guidance on what to do next.

callout.lead: Which is why one interface cannot serve both
callout.text: The failures are not different severities of the same problem. They point in opposite directions — one wants less interpretation, the other wants almost nothing but.

slides.notes: Read both lists. The audience needs to feel that these are genuinely opposing before the two-interface decision looks like anything other than scope creep.

slides.title: Two personas, built from opposing stakes

items.name: Type 1 diabetes patient
items.goal: Know the number, know where it is heading, act correctly, now
items.mindset: The stakes are medical. Ambiguity is dangerous, and this is often happening under stress.
needs: Trend direction legible at a glance
Alerts that are simple and actionable
Everything in one place, not scattered

items.name: Wellness consumer
items.goal: Understand whether today was good, and what to do differently
items.mindset: The stakes are motivational. Raw data demotivates; a single interpretable score sustains the habit.
needs: Cause and effect between food, exercise and glucose
Clear guidance on the next step

slides.notes: The mindset rows are the ones that matter. "Raw data demotivates" is the sentence that justifies the entire wellness interface.

slides.title: Two journeys: check-in, throughout the day, weekly review

rows.label: T1D · actions
cells: Open the app, read the current value and trend
Check repeatedly, respond to alerts, log insulin and food
Look back for patterns before a clinical appointment

rows.label: T1D · pain points
cells: Anxiety over a single number with no context
Uncertainty about what a trend means; logging events forgotten
Data scattered across screens, patterns hard to find

rows.label: Wellness · actions
cells: Check yesterday's outcome, look for a verdict
Log meals and exercise, hope for feedback

rows.label: Wellness · pain points

Disconnected data points, no real-time feedback on actions
No clear guidance on what to do next

slides.notes: This is dense. Read one column vertically rather than each row — it shows the two users diverging at the same moment in the day.

slides.title: For the T1D patient: clarity first
slides.standfirst: Prioritise critical data. Design for high-stress situations. Make trends legible at a glance.
slides.notes: Three principles, and they are ranked. Clarity first means literally first — anything competing with the current value loses.

slides.title: Three principles, applied strictly

bullets.text: Prioritise critical data with a bold, minimal design.
Design for high-stress situations by making alerts simple and actionable.
A colour-coded timeline making trends legible at a glance.

figure.alt: The redesigned T1D home screen with the current reading and trend arrow as focal point
figure.caption: Current reading and trend arrow as the focal point

slides.notes: Principles that do not force a trade-off are decoration. These three cost the home screen everything that was not the current value.

slides.title: Home and History, consolidated
slides.standfirst: One screen: the current reading and trend arrow as focal point, a full-width colour-coded 24-hour graph including a future glucose prediction, and a scrollable historical timeline beneath.

after.alt: The redesigned consolidated home and history screen
after.label: Redesigned

slides.notes: Consolidating home and history directly answers "data scattered across screens" from the journey map. Make that link explicitly.

slides.title: A forward prediction, so the user can plan rather than react
slides.standfirst: The 24-hour graph does not stop at now. Extending it forward turns a monitoring device into a planning one — which is the difference between managing glucose and chasing it.

bullets.text: Colour coding carries range at a glance, without reading values.
Full width, because the trend graph was the element the incumbent shrank.
Prediction is the answer to "uncertainty about what a trend means".

figure.caption: Solid history, dashed prediction, target band behind both

slides.notes: Same figure as slide two, used differently: earlier it was context, here it is the design decision. Say so, or it looks like a repeat.

slides.title: Alerts restructured for someone who is already stressed

bullets.text: Glucose alerts separated clearly from System alerts.
Each alert is a direct route to its setting.
Fast customisation, because the moment you need to change an alert is rarely a calm one.

figure.alt: The restructured alerts screen separating glucose from system alerts
figure.caption: Glucose above System, tappable rows, simple toggles

slides.notes: Alert configuration is where clinical apps usually hide their worst interaction design. Under-stress usability is the whole spec for this screen.

slides.title: For the wellness consumer: interpretation, not data
slides.standfirst: Gamified experience. Holistic view. Proactive coaching.
slides.notes: The pivot. Everything valued in part one — rawness, immediacy, precision — is the wrong answer here.

slides.title: One Metabolic Score, replacing disconnected data points
slides.standfirst: A prominent circular gauge presenting a single motivating metric. Not because the underlying data is less rich, but because a number you can compare with yesterday is a number you will come back for.

figure.label: Metabolic Score
figure.sub: One motivating metric, derived from the same stream
figure.caption: The gamified centrepiece of the wellness experience

slides.notes: The value shown is illustrative. The point is the form: circular, prominent, single, comparable.

slides.title: Gamified, holistic, proactive

bullets.text: A prominent circular gauge presenting the Metabolic Score as the motivating metric.
A correlation graph linking glucose trends to logged diet and exercise events, so cause and effect is visible directly.
AI-powered Insight of the Day and Smart Food Suggestions.

figure.alt: The wellness dashboard with the Metabolic Score
figure.caption: The wellness dashboard

slides.notes: Note the ordering: score first, then explanation, then advice. It matches the order a motivated non-clinical user actually asks questions in.

slides.title: Correlation, so an action has a visible consequence
slides.standfirst: Glucose trends plotted against logged diet and exercise events. This is the answer to "disconnected data points" and "no real-time feedback on actions" at the same time.

items.alt: The correlation graph linking glucose to logged events
items.label: Correlation

slides.notes: Correlation is the behaviour-change mechanism. Without it, a score is just a number that moves for reasons the user cannot influence.

slides.title: The wellness experience, screen by screen
slides.notes: AI coaching is the easiest thing in this deck to oversell. Frame it as interpretation of the user's own data, not as prediction.

slides.title: Two flows, one data layer — and one shared control
slides.standfirst: Both experiences share a simplified floating quick-add logging control, because forgotten logging was the one pain point both personas had in common.

slides.title: Two user groups sharing one data stream and inverting each other's priorities

bullets.text: Needs raw, immediate, unambiguous numbers, because the stakes are medical.
Needs those same numbers abstracted into a single interpretable score, because raw data demotivates them.

callout.text: Designing one product for both without diluting either required accepting divergent interfaces on a common foundation, rather than a unified compromise. An averaged interface would have failed both.

figure.alt: The challenge of two opposing users on one data stream

slides.notes: This is the thesis slide. If you have five minutes and one slide, use this one plus the personas.

slides.title: These are conceptual prototypes, not validated designs
slides.standfirst: Grounded in UX best practice and analysis of the provided materials — but produced without access to real users or usage data.

bullets.text: They serve as a starting point for discussion, not as an answer.
A real process would be driven by user interviews, usability testing and behavioural data analysis.
The Metabolic Score in particular is a design proposition that would need validating against outcomes, not just engagement.

slides.notes: Say this before anyone asks. Volunteering the limit is what makes the reasoning credible; being caught out on it undoes the whole deck.

slides.title: When two segments invert each other, the average serves neither
slides.standfirst: The instinct in platform design is to unify. But if one user needs raw precision and the other needs raw precision hidden, a single interface has to pick — and pretending otherwise just picks badly.

callout.text: Share the data layer, the logging model and the design system. Diverge at the surface, deliberately and visibly, and be able to say why for every point of divergence.
